name: Self-Consistency Bias
description: People can reconstruct their memories of past attitudes, feelings, or behavior so they look more consistent with who they believe they are now. The past gets edited toward the present self-story.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to retrospective interviews, journey reconstructions, habit-tracking reflections, onboarding 'before/after' storytelling, and any product that asks users to remember how they used to think or behave. Reported change may be distorted toward a coherent current identity.
myth_risk_note: The label 'self-consistency bias' is less canonical in the literature than the underlying reconstructive-memory research it draws on. This pass's discovery search did not surface new focused empirical tests of self-consistency bias specifically (candidates addressed confirmation bias in perceptual decisions, citation/publication bias, and unrelated methodology) -- assessment continues to rest on the existing corpus's McFarland & Ross (1987) backing, which directly supports the phenomenon (people overestimate how similar their past evaluations were to their current impressions).
prevalence_note: Mostly seen in cognitive-bias glossaries, identity/behavior-change writing, and research-methodology discussions about retrospective self-report; not a standard everyday UX checklist term.

findings.description: Across a two-session study of dating partners, participants reconstructed their earlier self, partner, and relationship evaluations toward their current impressions: when their current view had grown more positive, they remembered earlier ratings as more positive than they really were, and when their current view had grown more negative, they remembered earlier ratings as more negative. They also recalled their earlier causal attributions as having been more consistent with their current impressions than was actually the case, directly supporting a present-self-shaped memory for past attitudes and judgments.
findings.source_title: The Relation between Current Impressions and Memories of Self and Dating Partners
